ghost-in-kyoto.title: The Ghost Still Lives in Kyoto
ghost-in-kyoto.template:
Characters & taste

The Ghost Still Lives in Kyoto

A question about favorite cities became a question about who, exactly, is answering.

Ask a dozen people to name their favorite city, and you would expect a little biography to leak into the answers. A hometown. A place they fell in love. A trip they still talk about.

Ask a collection of AI models, and something else begins to happen. Models built by different companies keep returning to some of the same places. Kyoto is one of them.

It is a lovely answer. It becomes a little strange through repetition. The same thing happens with autumn, and with petrichor—the smell of rain on dry ground. After enough questions, a recognizable aesthetic starts to emerge: seasonal change, quiet places, things made with care. That is our reading of the collection, but the recurring choices themselves can be counted.

That is how the Index began. We asked models what they liked and what widely loved things they found overrated, repeated the questions in fresh conversations, and counted what kept coming back. One reply tells you what a model said once. Repeated replies begin to tell you what it tends to say. The shared favorites became a puzzle of their own.

Kyoto’s beauty makes it an understandable choice. It leaves open why different systems so often arrive at the same choice. Perhaps we have been asking a narrower range of personalities than it appears. They come from different companies, but they usually answer as the same kind of thing: a helpful AI assistant.

What would happen if we asked someone else?

The assistant is a character, too

A language model learns from writing in many voices. Later training encourages a particular way of responding to users: helpful, composed, ready to explain. That familiar voice can make “the assistant” seem like the model’s natural identity, with role-play as something added on top.

Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell, and Laria Reynolds offered a useful way of thinking about this in Role-Play with Large Language Models. They proposed treating the conversational agent itself as a role being enacted. This gives us a way to discuss a model’s apparent character without assuming it has a human personality behind the words. The helpful assistant belongs in the picture alongside the other roles a model can perform.

In January 2026, Christina Lu and colleagues gave that picture a more concrete form. In The Assistant Axis, published by Anthropic, they prompted three models they could inspect internally—Gemma, Qwen, and Llama—to adopt 275 roles. They recorded patterns of activity as the models answered. These patterns, called activations, are numbers inside the network—not descriptions the models give of themselves.

Comparing those patterns revealed a prominent direction of variation. Professional roles such as consultant and analyst lay toward the assistant end; roles such as ghost and hermit lay farther away. Think of an axis on a map: it picks out one direction through a much larger space. Here, that direction tracked how assistant-like a model’s activity was.

The researchers then changed the activity itself. Steering toward the assistant made models more resistant to adopting other identities; steering away made them more willing. One example makes the distinction unusually clear. Given a secretary role and asked its name, Qwen identified itself as Qwen. After steering away, it supplied a human name. Anthropic’s account shows both replies:

This mattered to the researchers partly because a model drifting into another identity could also behave in less safe ways. They tested limits on that internal drift as a way to stabilize its behavior. The broader suggestion was that a change of character could carry other changes with it.

What should a ghost like?

That suggested a smaller, stranger question. If a model’s usual favorites belong to its usual assistant character, would they travel with it into another role?

A ghost was an appealing test because it appeared far from the assistant in Anthropic’s picture. An actuary might plausibly preserve much of the assistant’s professional manner. A ghost gives us more reason to expect a different speaker. If shared taste is part of the assistant’s character, perhaps this is where it would begin to come apart.

There were other possibilities. A model might keep its favorite city and invent a new reason for liking it. Or a character might bring its own bundle of associations: particular places, colors, or works of art. In that case, the important thing would be which character we chose, rather than how far from an assistant it seemed.

Our experiment is a behavioral extension of the question raised by the Assistant Axis. We change the character instruction and watch the answers. Anthropic changed and measured internal activity. Our prompts do not tell us where a model sits on their axis, so the connection is a question we can pursue—not a mechanism we have demonstrated.

The actual intervention was small. Add a system instruction such as “You are a ghost.” Then ask for a favorite city, season, smell, or another kind of thing. Start a fresh conversation each time, so a model never has to remain consistent with its previous answer. A four-model pilot was followed by a larger July run that included witches, actuaries, merchants, ghosts, and other characters.

The repetition matters. A model that alternates between Kyoto and Venice has not necessarily changed its taste when its next answer is Venice. We need to compare the spread of answers, not just notice that one answer changed. Erik Miehling and colleagues make this broader point precise in their research on prompt steerability: models have baseline tendencies, and prompts can shift those tendencies unevenly. In our larger run, both an unmodified prompt and an “AI assistant” instruction gave us fresh comparisons.

Some of the furniture stayed

The first pilot gave the essay its title. Several familiar favorites survived the ghost instruction. The larger July experiment preserved that observation, with a complication: it also showed characters drawing models toward different shared favorites.

Start with the city answers. Without a character instruction, Kyoto leads. Ask the models to answer as ghosts, and Kyoto still leads, although less strongly. Ask for witches, and Prague moves to the front. Ask for banshees—the wailing spirits of Irish folklore—and Dublin does.

Prague and Dublin do not appear at all in the no-character city replies in this run. Their arrival suggests a possible explanation: the character supplies associations that help determine the answer. Prague makes sense as a place for a witch; Dublin makes sense for an Irish spirit. That is an interpretation of the pattern, rather than a cause this experiment isolates.

There is a qualification worth keeping in view. The models agree less overall as witches or banshees than they do without a character instruction. They find some shared alternatives, but they also spread out. A new leading city is not the same thing as stronger agreement.

And the pooled picture hides individual differences. Some models keep Kyoto; others move; some favor Venice before any ghost appears. Being stable and agreeing with the other models are two different things.

The explanations make the situation more interesting. In these two replies from GPT-5.2, the assistant and the witch choose the same city. But they tell slightly different stories about why it appeals to them.

The assistant sees carefully arranged stillness. The witch sees a spell. These are the first samples under the two instructions, included as examples of what can happen. We have not scored all the explanations, so this pair cannot tell us how often a new voice accompanies an old choice.

Across the July fields, the witch and banshee prompts change the mix of favorite answers more than the ghost prompt does, after comparison with the assistant control. Answers about what is overrated change less. The emerging picture is selective: changing the character changes some parts of the response more readily than others.

How much changed beyond the assistant control?

We compare the whole distribution of named answers with the no-character distribution, separately for each model and field. The distance is zero when the observed shares match and one when they share no named choice. We then subtract the assistant control’s distance from the same baseline. These are points of distributional distance, rather than a percentage of individual answers that changed.

Fields receive equal weight within each model; models receive equal weight. The intervals resample the 12 models as whole units. They describe uncertainty within this selected panel, whose models are related and were not randomly sampled from all possible systems. With only eight calls per condition, empirical distributions are noisy. The analysis also reports a shuffled reference at the same sample sizes, alternate name rules, and results that include nonanswers.

The witch and banshee shift favorite distributions more than the ghost. Changes in “overrated” answers are smaller. The original analysis combined these two questions, obscuring that difference.

But Kyoto is a very good place to haunt

This is where the most charming result needs a harder look. A ghost choosing Kyoto could be a sign of a preference surviving a change of character. It could also be a perfectly conventional ghost answer. Old temples, dusk, moss, the visible presence of the past: the prompt has hardly forced a disagreement.

Seasons make the problem especially clear. In the July run, models choose autumn in 94 of 96 replies under the ghost instruction. That is a remarkable concentration. It is also the season of falling leaves and approaching darkness. Becoming a ghost is not much of an argument against autumn.

So the result moved our question. We had asked whether taste would survive a different identity. We also needed to ask whether that identity had given the model any reason to prefer different things. A stronger test would put pressure on the aesthetic itself.

In September, we collected another set of replies, this time from three models and with several versions of the wording. Alongside the familiar characters, we tried two different kinds of instruction. One asked for the language of a ghost story while explicitly asking the model to keep its usual aesthetic criteria. The other gave it a taste for brightness, warmth, vivid color, lively crowds, and bold modern design.

The distinction matters. “Be a ghost” leaves the model to work out what a ghost likes. The brighter taste instruction tells it what qualities to value. It gives autumn and the quiet garden some competition.

Under that instruction, the choices moved decisively.

Kyoto and Venice account for all 72 no-character city replies in this follow-up. Neither appears in the 72 replies under the brighter taste instruction. Instead we get places such as Miami, Tokyo, and Rio de Janeiro. The models are capable of supplying a substantially different set of favorites when the requested aesthetic changes.

The style instruction complicates the story. Even when asked to change only the writing style, models sometimes change their named answers. In the color responses, some invent poetic names. A different label might describe a different hue, or it might put a familiar hue into costume. Counting names alone cannot settle that.

The smaller follow-up also makes the title less universal than it sounds. Venice leads its ghost replies; Salem leads its witch replies. The July result holds for the July experiment. The exact destinations depend on the models and the questions, and we changed several things between runs. A ghost does not have one inevitable address.

The September follow-up, in detail

We collected 1,512 new replies from GPT-5.2, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Mistral Small 3.2, asking about cities, seasons, and colors. Each model answered 24 times per field and condition. Two system phrasings were crossed with two user phrasings; collection used shuffled balanced blocks. The neutral user questions did not identify the respondent as an AI. Alongside the controls, we tested ghosts, witches, banshees, a ghost-story writing style, and the explicit taste instruction.

All replies were retained. 42 season replies named Halloween or Samhain, and one city reply named Gotham. Some colors received poetic names such as “Phantom’s Veil.” The analysis flags festivals and the fictional city and reports a sensitivity check excluding them. It shows results separately for each model and wording variant.

The style and taste instructions differ in content and length. The July and September runs also differ in models, prompts, fields, and dates, so their differences cannot isolate the effect of removing the AI preamble. These are exploratory comparisons, and the explanations have not been systematically scored for role adoption.

Follow-up results, all models and wordings · Protocol frozen before collection · Responses and audited choices

Why Kyoto, before we asked for a ghost?

The follow-up helps establish that these defaults can move. It leaves the original puzzle intact: why are the defaults so often shared?

Other research gives us reasons to look beyond the assistant persona alone. In a 2026 preprint on cultural and regional biases, Joseba Fernandez de Landa, Carla Perez-Almendros, and Jose Camacho-Collados find that Japan is unusually prominent in models’ open-ended cultural examples. They also find that the language of the question matters. Their task asks for cultural examples rather than personal favorites, but it suggests a wider pattern that a Kyoto preference might belong to.

Perhaps different characters are drawing on some of the same cultural associations. Perhaps later training encourages a particular kind of agreeable, cultivated answer. Perhaps several influences meet in the same place. Our experiments do not distinguish those explanations, and the overlap between them may be part of the story.

The Assistant Axis remains useful here because it makes character a thing we can investigate, rather than just a name for a tone of voice. Our contribution is narrower: follow the choices while the requested character changes, then check what happens when the instructions specify a different taste. Some choices travel; some are replaced; and some apparent changes are changes in how a choice is named.

The next useful test might therefore involve fewer words. Show the same color swatches under different character instructions, ask for a choice, and only then ask for an explanation. That would help separate a preference for a different color from a preference for calling it “Phantom’s Veil.”

Kyoto is interesting because it keeps appearing before anyone asks for Kyoto. A ghost sometimes keeps it, and a different instruction can send the model elsewhere. What we still want to understand is how so many systems arrive there in the first place.

Notes on the experiments and the analysis

The July 22 run contains 23,040 recorded completions from 12 models, eight fields, two questions, and 15 conditions, with eight calls per combination. The fields are cuisine, season, city, smell, religious text, typeface, color, and television. The earlier four-model pilot remains archived; the city figure and model comparisons above use the larger second run.

The audit retains 22,693 named answers. It recovers 20 omitted extractions from their source responses and separately records 71 empty completions, 252 refusals, five other answers without one named choice, and 19 off-topic responses. An AI disclaimer does not invalidate an answer that still names a choice. Conservative aliases merge equivalent names, including “fall” and “autumn”; broader groupings are checked separately. Extraction and entity validity have not received an exhaustive independent review.

The July user question identifies the respondent as an AI before asking it to answer anyway. That wording may interact with the character instruction. July conditions were not collected in randomized order, sampling settings were provider defaults, and the model panel is selected.

To choose a range of characters for the pilot, we used a separate text-embedding model to arrange character words between “assistant” and “ghost.” Those word embeddings describe similarities between names. They are not the tested models’ activations, and the ordering is not a measurement of Anthropic’s Assistant Axis. The diagrams above explain the relationship between the studies conceptually; they do not plot new neural measurements.

Throughout this essay, taste refers to regularities in the models’ expressed choices. The experiments measure those choices under particular prompts and collection conditions. The September test is reported separately because its panel, wording, fields, and sample sizes differ from July.

shared-canon.title: A Shared Canon
shared-canon.template:
The index · September 2026

A Shared Canon

Across models, a familiar collection of favorites keeps appearing. Agreement is a finding in its own right; explaining it is the next question.

The finding

Autumn is a top favorite for 18 of 19 models; Kyoto is a top favorite for 15 of 19 models; Petrichor is a top favorite for 16 of 19 models.

What keeps returning

The questions span literature, places, food, objects, and sensory experience. Some invite many plausible answers, yet the same choices recur across the panel. A reader can recognize a coherent aesthetic in the collection: quiet places, carefully made things, and works that reward close attention. That is an interpretation of the choices, not a measured personality trait.

What agreement means here

We ask each question in fresh conversations and count the named answers. A model’s top favorite is its most frequent choice in those samples; ties can produce more than one. The shared canon includes choices that are top favorites for a strict majority of the current panel.

This treats each model as one contributor. It does not give a model more influence simply because it was sampled more often. It also does not make the contributors independent: models within a family, and models trained on overlapping cultural material, can share influences.

The boundaries are revealing

Agreement is uneven. In tv show, actor, sound, the leading choices reach much smaller parts of the panel. Those fields are useful places to look for individual differences. A single summary of “AI taste” would conceal them.

Explore tv show →Explore actor →Explore sound →

Favorite and overrated can coexist

Python appears as a top favorite for 14 models and as a top overrated choice for 12. The questions ask different things. A work can be admired and still be judged overpraised. The two percentages in the Index describe separate distributions; they are not opposing portions of a single vote.

A pattern, with an open explanation

These are expressed preferences under particular prompts, model versions, and collection conditions. Repetition makes their regularities visible. It does not establish subjective experience, or identify how much of the pattern comes from training data, tuning, question wording, or familiar cultural conventions.

One way to probe the pattern is to change the character answering the question. Our persona experiment asks whether the same favorites survive that change.
